# A virtual store: BRAN2023 on THREDDS {#sec-virtual}

```{r}
#| include: false
source("R/book.R")
```

Most of the world's gridded data is not Zarr and will not be rewritten as
Zarr. It is NetCDF and HDF5, in archives, served as files. A *virtual*
Zarr store leaves those files alone and keeps a table of references: for
each chunk, which file, which byte offset, how many bytes. Kerchunk and
VirtualiZarr write such tables; zaro reads them (kerchunk JSON and
Parquet, VirtualiZarr Parquet manifests, byterefs tables) and from then on
the store behaves like any other.

BRAN2023 is CSIRO's Bluelink ocean reanalysis: daily fields at 51 depths
on a 0.1 degree global grid, 2010 to 2024, about 11 TB of NetCDF on NCI's
THREDDS server. A VirtualiZarr reference store for it lives
[on GitHub](https://github.com/mdsumner/virtualized). Temperature is one
array of 3600 x 1500 x 51 x 5479 values in chunks of 300 x 300 x 1 x 1:
each chunk is a tile of one depth on one day, a few tens of kilobytes
inside a monthly NetCDF file.

```r
bran <- zaro("virtualizarr://https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mdsumner/virtualized/refs/heads/main/remote/ocean_temp_2023.parq")
temp <- zaro_array(bran, "temp", cf = TRUE)    # degrees C
dim(temp)
#> [1] 3600 1500   51 5479
```

No NetCDF library is involved, and nothing is copied.

## The reads

A surface map for one day (60 chunks, all in one file); a profile at one
cell (51 chunks, one per depth); a north-south section by depth; and a
month of surface values at one cell.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
#| file: scripts/04-virtual.R
```

```{r}
res <- book_run("04-virtual.R", live = TRUE)
book_table(res)
```

This store shows something the native Zarr store could not. When zaro is
given a whole batch, it looks at the byte ranges, and ranges that touch in
the same file are merged into one request. The 60 tiles of a surface map
sit end to end in the NetCDF file, so a planned read of the map can be a
single HTTP request. Asked one chunk at a time, there is nothing to merge:
60 requests to a THREDDS server, in series.

So here the **Requests** column can differ between builds, while **MB**
stays the same. Fewer, larger requests are kinder to an archive server
than many small ones, as well as faster for the reader. The patch is what
lets R be the polite client.

```{r}
book_elt(res)
```

## A track is already fine

One read from this store needs no patch: values along a track, one
(x, y, depth, day) per row, is a matrix subscript (@sec-points). A 30-day
track off Tasmania was 30 byte ranges from 30 files, one fetch call, 2 MB
in half a second (measured 2026-10-03). The profile and the section above
are the same data asked for as rectangles, and that is the only reason
they fare differently.
